newsitem.title: USA: "Spring break court" controls Florida revelers.
newsitem.headline: "Spring break court" controls Florida revelers.

text.p: As college students throng the streets of Key West on their annual spring break, city authorities have set up a special court to mete out swift punishment to revellers who run afoul of the law.

Arrests, mostly for under-age drinking, were expected to peak this week as students flock in from colleges across the country to soak up the tropical atmosphere and cruise the many bars. They rule the streets on their rented scooters by day while at night police watch for trouble outside Sloppy Joe's Bar on Duval Street where Ernest Hemingway once drank.

Arrests declined from 466 in 1994 to 267 last year thanks in part to the special "Spring Break Court." By far the most common offence is trying to sneak into a bar with a fake or borrowed drivers license as "proof" of age. Florida's legal drinking age is 21, while many of the students are 20 or younger.
Lt. John Szabo of the state divison of alcoholic beverages and tobacco said 104 fake IDs had been confiscated so far in Key West this spring break.

Until 1992, young offenders were hauled off to jail as soon as they were caught and left to mull their crimes overnight until they appeared in court. But the jail became too small to hold the revellers and the county paid an undisclosed cash settlement to settle a suit by several female students who were strip searched, so Key West police stopped jailing their young visitors.

Instead, they order them to appear at the special spring break court at 8 a.m. the next morning. It sits every day, including Sunday. In court, the judge gives each violator the choice of paying a $175 fine or performing eight hours of community service wearing a bright orange smock with the words "Monroe County Jail" emblazoned on its back.

Most students choose the community service, often after Judge Wayne Miller reminds them the court does not accept credit cards -- not even daddy's. "It's not like Sears," he said during Sunday morning's session.

Some of this week's smock-clad students were resigned to spending eight hours of their vacation performing community service. "It's $175 and I'm already strapped for cash on spring break," said Purdue senior Derek Moon, 23, who was picking up litter near a popular beach.
But others were angry, saying police should expend their energy on crimes worse than spring break high spirits.

"They've got nothing better to do than harass us. We're out here finding heroin needles in the bushes," said Chris Weymouth, 19, a student at Western Carolina University, who was arrested for public drinking.
Some students want to keep their smocks after finishing their service but Miller reminds the students they are not for sale.
